title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM + CUDA graphs - deep dive (Cosmica Systems)
summary: Redwood SE team walked Cosmica Systems through GPU runtime profiling approach: kernel selection heuristics, measured comparison between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM for their 8k context classification workload, benefits and pitfalls of CUDA graphs, KV cache eviction patterns, batching knobs, and quantization impact on latency/quality. Customer is interested in an on-prem pilot and a short benchmark run on their 4xA100 fleet.
next_steps: Redwood to share profiling runbook and perf dashboard link
Customer to provide sample traces + model artifact (quantized and fp16)
Schedule 2-hour on-prem benchmark window week of 2026-02-28
action_items: Leo Ramirez: share CUDA graphs demo notebook and nvprof traces - due 2026-02-18
Arun Patel: export 10 representative request traces and model weights (fp16 + int8) - due 2026-02-20
Maya Chen: send pilot contract template and pricing estimate for 4xA100 reserved capacity - due 2026-02-19
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we wanted to do a deep dive on the GPU runtime profiling work we ran and how it applies to Cosmica's 8k context classification workload. um leo will lead on the kernel selection bits.
[00:12] Leo Ramirez: yeah thanks maya, hi arun, sofia, victor. quick agenda: kernel selection heuristics, tRT-LLM vs vLLM bench, cuda graphs patterns, kv cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, deployment notes for on-prem/VPC.
[00:28] Arun Patel: hey sorry for the delay, we had a pager, excited to see numbers. our main pain is unpredictable tail latency when concurrency spikes. cost is also a big factor.
[00:40] Sofia Martinez: and we run on 4xA100s in our colo, currently using a Triton-based stack plus some in-house batching logic, so curious how Redwood's runtime would fit.
[00:52] Leo Ramirez: perfect context. quick note — transcription may mismatch some product names, e.g., we say TensorRT-LLM sometimes, tRT-LLM in slides.
[01:04] Priya Singh: ok jumping in on kernel selection: our profiling flow picks kernels by a cost model: measured ms per op across representative seq lengths, then picks lowest-latency implementation given memory constraints. for attention we compare fused vs unfused kernel variants, and for matmuls we test tensor core vs fp16 fallback.
[01:28] Sofia Martinez: can you explain fused vs unfused? we saw different terms in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[01:34] Leo Ramirez: sure, fused attention merges multiple steps (q,k,v projections, matmul, softmax) into a single kernel to reduce global memory ops. unfused breaks them so you can reuse cached kvs more flexibly, sometimes better at very long contexts. often fused wins on latency up to ~4k but on 8k the memory pressure flips it.
[01:56] Victor Lee: that matches our observation — tail latency spikes at ~6k tokens, we thought kv cache thrashing might be the cause.
[02:06] Leo Ramirez: exactly, kv cache eviction and page faults on the GPU can cause microsecond -> millisecond tail events. we instrumented per-layer kv cache hit/miss rates in our run.
[02:18] Arun Patel: how did you measure cache eviction? did you use nvprof or our profiler?
[02:24] Priya Singh: we used a combination: nvprof/cupti for low-level kernel timings and a lightweight tracer in the runtime to log kv allocation events. attaching the nvprof samples is in the runbook link we'll share.
[02:36] Maya Chen: (interrupting) also note we tested both TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) and vLLM in the same hardware profile, same model converted to TensorRT where possible.
[02:48] Sofia Martinez: ok results please.
[02:52] Leo Ramirez: high level: for single-request P95 latency, TensorRT-LLM (with optimized kernels) was ~12% faster on avg than vLLM when model ops were supported by TRT. however vLLM had much more predictable behavior under mixed concurrency because of its async batching and better kv cache locality on our workload.
[03:16] Priya Singh: important caveat: TRT-LLM shines when you can compile everything into fused kernels and avoid fallback paths; but for models with dynamic shapes or many custom ops, you hit fallback kernels which degrade results. we saw a 30% regression in latency when 2 small custom ops caused fallback to generic CUDA kernels.
[03:38] Arun Patel: hmm we have a couple custom ops for tokenization / scoring. will those break TRT?
[03:44] Leo Ramirez: potentially — tokenizers usually live on CPU, but scoring that is inside model graph could. we recommended isolating custom ops into separate postprocessing steps or implementing them as TRT plugins.
[03:56] Victor Lee: about cuda graphs — we saw a slide earlier that said cuda graphs reduce CPU overhead. how brittle are they for bursty workloads?
[04:04] Priya Singh: cuda graphs are great: they capture a sequence of kernel launches and replay them with near-zero CPU overhead. that reduces latency variance a lot for steady pipelines. but they are brittle when control flow changes (e.g., variable batch sizes or model branches). we used a hybrid approach: small set of pre-captured graphs for the common batch sizes plus a fallback path.
[04:26] Sofia Martinez: how do you handle dynamic sequence lengths and batching with cuda graphs?
[04:30] Leo Ramirez: we capture graphs for expected seq length buckets (e.g., <512, 512-2048, 2k-8k). runtime selects nearest bucket and pads to match graph shape. padding costs are often less than kernel launch overhead for heavy models. we also keep a fast fallback that uses standard launches.
[04:50] Maya Chen: note on cost: cuda graphs plus fused kernels gave the best cost per token in our tests, but only if the workload fits capture buckets. for truly ad-hoc lengths, vLLM's dynamic batching was more cost-effective.
[05:06] Arun Patel: can you share numbers on throughput? e.g., tokens/sec at 8k context with concurrency 4?
[05:12] Leo Ramirez: on 4xA100 with TRT-LLM compiled model, we measured ~1.6M tokens/min (~26.6k tokens/sec total aggregate) at concurrency 4 with steady streams, vLLM was ~1.3M tokens/min in same setup but with 10-15% lower tail variance. these are indicative — we'll share raw dashboards.
[05:32] Victor Lee: what about KV cache size and memory? we currently store full fp16 kvs and run out at large batch sizes.
[05:40] Priya Singh: kv cache memory grows with seq_len * hidden_size * 2 (for k/v) * batch. we use quantized kv storage (int8) for longer contexts to reduce memory approx 2-4x depending on quantization scheme. int8 kv gave ~30% memory saving but introduced slight quality delta in very sensitive classification thresholds.
[06:00] Arun Patel: any guidance on quantization tradeoffs? we're worried about classification probability calibration.
[06:06] Leo Ramirez: yes — for classification where small logits shifts matter, prefer fp16 for kv and only quantize embeddings or less-sensitive parts. for LLM generation or summarization int8 kv often acceptable. we recommend running comparison evals on your calibration set.
[06:20] Sofia Martinez: on-prem notes: we need VPC integration and key management. what does Redwood need from us to run the pilot?
[06:28] Maya Chen: for Private on-prem pilot we need: access window for 2 hours for benchmarking, SSH jump with restricted accounts, KMS endpoint details for model keys if encrypting, and sample traces. we'll use a read-only monitoring agent for perf metrics.
[06:40] Arun Patel: we can provide those. security doc?
[06:43] Maya Chen: yes we'll attach SOC2 compliance pack and the private deployment security checklist; see link in chat (https://redwood-inference.example/docs/security-pack).
[06:54] Victor Lee: one more thing — how do you handle preemption if we use spot capacity for cost reasons? we want graceful degradation.
[06:59] Priya Singh: runtime supports multi-tier routing: primary reserved nodes + spot pool. on preemption we drain and re-route to compatible model variant (smaller quantized model) to keep requests alive. that gives graceful quality degradation rather than dropped requests.
[07:14] Leo Ramirez: also, we can configure per-route SLOs and automatic fallback policies. for instance your critical classification route can have a strict latency SLO pinned to reserved capacity while non-critical batch jobs use spot.
[07:28] Maya Chen: quick recap and next steps?
[07:30] Arun Patel: yeah long list but top things: run pilot on our 4xA100s, evaluate fp16 vs int8 kv on our cal set, and validate cuda graphs stability for our seq distributions.
[07:42] Maya Chen: actions: we'll share profiling runbook and CUDA notebook (leo). arun you'll share traces and model artifacts. we schedule 2-hour benchmark week of 2/28. maya will send contract/price.
[07:55] Sofia Martinez: sounds good. please also include instrumentation hooks so our SREs can pull perf metrics.
[08:02] Priya Singh: will do — we'll include prometheus exporters + tracing hooks.
[08:07] Victor Lee: thanks all.
[08:09] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. end of recording.

Notes: transcript contains typical ASR mistakes; some technical terms abbreviated (TRT-LLM, tRT, vLLM). Dashboard link and runbook will be posted in CRM.
